---
title: "Semantic review"
description: "Decide the ontology IRIs and fill in the free-text metadata from Python, without opening a CSV in a spreadsheet."
---

`create_sdp()` gives you a package that is **review-ready, not finished**. Two
calls take it the rest of the way, and both print the exact call for the next
step — you paste it, and the script you end up with is the record of what you
decided.

**A package can reach `validate_salmon_datapackage(require_iris=True)` without
opening a single file in a spreadsheet.** Editing `metadata/*.csv` by hand still
works and is still supported; it is the [fallback](#the-spreadsheet-fallback)
rather than the recommended path, because a spreadsheet edit leaves no record of
*why* a term was chosen, and that record is the most valuable thing the review
produces.

## Decide the semantic IRIs

`review_semantics()` builds a re-runnable queue from suggestions that already
exist: one entry per unfilled semantic slot, each with its ranked shortlist and
the exact call that decides it.

```python
from metasalmonpy import review_semantics

review = review_semantics(package_path)
review
```

```
── spawners · spawner_count · variable ───────────────────────────────────────
   field:   column_dictionary.csv · term_iri
   current: REVIEW:https://w3id.org/smn/SpawnerAbundance

   [1] Spawner Abundance   smn   score 4.9
       The number of mature salmon returning to spawn in a stream.
       https://w3id.org/smn/SpawnerAbundance
       review = accept_suggestion(review, "spawner_count", "variable", rank=1)

       review = reject_suggestion(review, "spawner_count", "variable")   # no candidate fits

── spawners · entity ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   field:   tables.csv · observation_unit_iri
   current: <blank>

   [1] Spawner Abundance   smn   score 4.9
       The number of mature salmon returning to spawn in a stream.
       https://w3id.org/smn/SpawnerAbundance
       review = accept_suggestion(review, role="entity", rank=1, table="spawners")

       review = reject_suggestion(review, role="entity", table="spawners")   # no candidate fits

── next ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   0 of 9 slots decided.
   Paste the calls above into your script, then write the decisions:
   apply_sdp_semantics("catch-sdp", review)
```

**This never contacts a network or an LLM.** It reads the
`semantic_suggestions` attribute, or `semantic_suggestions.csv`, that
`suggest_semantics()` / `create_sdp()` already produced. Where those suggestions
carry LLM review — only possible if they were generated with `llm_assess=True` —
it surfaces it; it never generates it.

`review_semantics()` accepts a written package path, a dictionary carrying the
attribute, or the mapping `infer_salmon_datapackage_artifacts()` returns.
`include_filled=True` also queues slots that already hold a final IRI or already
carry a decision, `max_candidates=` bounds the shortlist per slot (`None` shows
all), and `columns=` restricts the queue — a name matching no column is an error
naming the columns that do exist, because filtering first and reporting an empty
queue told a user who mistyped a column name that their package was finished.

### Accept, or reject with a reason

Both take a review and return a new one, so a whole review is an ordinary,
re-runnable script. Nothing is written until `apply_sdp_semantics()` runs.

```python
from metasalmonpy import accept_suggestion, apply_sdp_semantics, reject_suggestion

review = accept_suggestion(review, "spawner_count", "variable", rank=1)
review = reject_suggestion(
    review,
    "spawner_count",
    "unit",
    reason="Counts of fish are dimensionless; no QUDT unit applies.",
)

apply_sdp_semantics(package_path, review)
```

The address arguments follow the slot, and `review_semantics()` always prints
the right spelling: omit `column` for a table-level slot and pass `table=`
instead; pass `table=` as well when a column name appears in more than one
table; pass `code_value=` for a `codes.csv` slot. Where the right term exists
but retrieval never surfaced it, accept it directly with
`accept_suggestion(review, "spawner_count", "variable", iri="…")`.

**`reason=` is written into the package**, as `semantic_suggestions.csv`'s
`decision_reason` column, and `review_metadata()` reads it back onto the gap the
rejection left:

```
   unit_iri: required IRI and not yet decided
      you rejected every candidate here: Counts of fish are dimensionless; no
      QUDT unit applies.
```

Without it that gap comes back looking exactly like one nobody ever considered.

`apply_sdp_semantics()` is surgical and safe to re-run: it strips the `REVIEW:`
prefix from the fields you decided, leaves undecided slots and their markers
alone, and does not touch a byte of your data CSVs. The metadata CSVs,
`semantic_suggestions.csv` and `datapackage.json` install as one transactional
set, because the descriptor duplicates the dictionary's IRI fields and a
half-applied edit would leave the package quietly self-inconsistent. Decisions
persist, so you can stop and pick the review up tomorrow without being asked the
same questions again.

## Fill in the free text, and the slots with no candidates

`review_metadata()` reads the package against the rules that actually decide
strict validation rather than against a shortlist, so it sees something the
semantic review structurally cannot: **a required field that no candidate was
ever found for**. `review_semantics()` builds its queue from retrieved
suggestions, so a slot nothing was found for never appears there; an empty
shortlist and a full one look the same to `review_metadata()`.

```python
from metasalmonpy import review_metadata, set_sdp_dataset

review_metadata(package_path)
```

```
── dataset.csv ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   description: placeholder text, refused by strict validation
      MISSING DESCRIPTION: describe the contents and purpose of dataset
      'demo-1'.
   creator: placeholder text, refused by strict validation
      MISSING METADATA: add creator, team, or originating program.

   set_sdp_dataset("catch-sdp",
     description="<describe the contents and purpose of dataset 'demo-1'>",
     creator="<add creator, team, or originating program>"
   )

── next ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   13 fields still block strict validation.
   Replace each <...> with the real value, then paste the calls above.
   4 of them are IRIs -- review_semantics() shows candidates for any that have them.
   Then: validate_salmon_datapackage("catch-sdp", require_iris=True)
```

What it reports: unresolved `MISSING DESCRIPTION:` / `MISSING METADATA:` /
`REVIEW REQUIRED:` placeholders; schema-required fields
(`constraints.required`) that are blank, where a column the file does not have
counts as blank in every row; any schema-declared `*_iri` field of
`tables.csv`, `column_dictionary.csv` or `codes.csv` still carrying an
unresolved `REVIEW:` marker; measurement columns missing `term_iri`,
`property_iri`, `entity_iri` or `unit_iri`; and `tables.csv` rows with a blank
`observation_unit_iri`. It never contacts a network or an LLM, and the schema it
reads `constraints.required` from is the bundled copy rather than the remote
one.

### The four setters

```python
from metasalmonpy import set_sdp_code, set_sdp_column, set_sdp_dataset, set_sdp_table

set_sdp_dataset(
    package_path,
    description="Spawner counts for two Vancouver Island streams, 2024.",
    creator="Salmon Data Mobilization",
    contact_name="Data steward",
    contact_email="steward@example.org",
    license="CC-BY-4.0",
)
set_sdp_table(
    package_path,
    "spawners",
    description="One row per stream per survey year.",
    observation_unit="A stream-year spawner count.",
    observation_unit_iri="https://w3id.org/smn/Observation",
)
set_sdp_column(
    package_path,
    "spawner_count",
    table="spawners",
    column_description="Count of mature spawners observed in the stream.",
    unit_iri="https://qudt.org/vocab/unit/INDIV",
)
set_sdp_code(
    package_path,
    "stream_name",
    "Goldstream",
    table="spawners",
    code_description="Goldstream River, Vancouver Island.",
)
```

Each addresses one row, writes the named fields into it, and keeps
`datapackage.json` in step in the same transactional write. Every field the SDP
schema declares for the file can be set: the ones most often unfilled are named
arguments for discoverability, and the rest pass through `**extras` and are
checked against the schema, so a misspelled `licence=` is an error rather than a
silent no-op. Pass `None` for a field you are not setting, `pandas.NA` to clear
one deliberately; a blank string is refused as ambiguous.

**Pasting a printed call unedited is refused.** A package whose `creator` reads
`<add creator, team, or originating program>` would pass strict validation while
saying nothing, which is worse than the placeholder it replaced, because the
marker is gone.

Use `set_sdp_column(..., term_iri="…")` for a slot retrieval found no candidate
for, and `accept_suggestion()` when there is a shortlist to choose from.

### Then strict validation passes

When `review_metadata()` reports nothing outstanding:

```python
from metasalmonpy import validate_salmon_datapackage

validate_salmon_datapackage(package_path, require_iris=True)
```

For an interactive, resumable whole-variable review, use
`chat_decomposition()`. It persists structured state and never submits a term
request automatically.

## Deterministic suggestions

`suggest_semantics()` searches for candidates for dictionary, code, table, and
dataset targets. Measurement columns use six ordered semantic roles:
variable, property, entity, unit, constraint, and statistical modifier.

There is no dictionary *method* slot. sdp-0.3.0 removed it: a method is how
a value was produced, not part of what the value **is**, so it moved to the
three placements `migrate_sdp_methods()` relocates it to. The `method` role
survives only for `codes.csv` term targets — a code value naming a
procedure.

```python
from metasalmonpy import infer_dictionary, semantic_suggestions, suggest_semantics

dictionary = infer_dictionary(
    observations,
    dataset_id="catch-monitoring",
    table_id="observations",
)

reviewed = suggest_semantics(
    observations,
    dictionary,
    sources=["smn", "gcdfo"],
    max_per_role=3,
)

suggestions = semantic_suggestions(reviewed)
```

When `sources` is omitted, metasalmonpy chooses role-aware defaults. An explicitly
supplied source list is a strict allowlist for initial and retry retrieval.
For example, `sources="smn"` cannot introduce QUDT candidates.

`semantic_suggestions()` and its companion `semantic_llm_assessments()` are the
supported way to read what a stage attached, so review tooling never reaches
into `df.attrs` itself. Both accept a dictionary, an artifact mapping, or a
written package path, and both return `None` rather than an empty frame when
nothing is attached — they replace a raw `attrs` lookup and must answer an
`is None` test the same way it did. A package path always returns `None` from
`semantic_llm_assessments()`: assessments are not written into the package, so a
package on disk cannot carry them.

## LLM review is opt-in

Context does not enable an LLM call. You must set `llm_assess=True` explicitly.
Context file inputs must be local paths, not parsed pandas, XML, or document
objects.

```python
reviewed = suggest_semantics(
    observations,
    dictionary,
    sources=["smn"],
    llm_assess=True,
    llm_provider="openrouter",
    llm_model="openai/gpt-5.4-mini",
    llm_context_files=["data_dictionary.csv"],
)

assessments = semantic_llm_assessments(reviewed)
```

Supplying `llm_context_files` or `llm_context_text` while
`llm_assess=False` produces a warning and makes no provider request.

## Bundle review

Measurement targets are reviewed as one column bundle. The request contains the
original dictionary row, existing semantics, value metadata, all six candidate
slots, relevant context, and the retrieval-source policy.

The adapter preserves the public per-target format:

- `semantic_suggestions` remains the candidate table;
- `semantic_llm_assessments` always uses the same 30-column schema;
- positional candidate indices remain available to callers;
- provider failures retain the deterministic shortlist; and
- malformed individual slots fall back without discarding valid sibling slots.

Retry processing is bounded to one round. An exact retry of the original query
is preserved as a `retry_search` decision, marked with
`llm_retry_query_rejection_reason="duplicate_original_query"`, and skipped.
Near-duplicate queries remain eligible. Escalated shortlist rejections retain
`llm_escalated_from="reject_shortlist"`.

## Deterministic validators

Pure validators can downgrade unsupported `accept` decisions to `review` for:

- missing method evidence;
- missing constraint evidence;
- role and ontology-type incompatibility;
- deterministically known unit/property dimensional conflicts; and
- curated semantic redundancy.

A downgrade clears the selected candidate but preserves model confidence and
rationale as provenance. Validators never retrieve, substitute, or invent
terms.

## Applying a whole batch at once

`review_semantics()` decides one slot at a time and is the recommended path.
`apply_semantic_suggestions()` is the batch alternative, for a dictionary you
have not written yet:

```python
from metasalmonpy import apply_semantic_suggestions

updated = apply_semantic_suggestions(
    reviewed,
    strategy="llm",
    roles=["variable", "property", "entity", "unit"],
    min_llm_confidence=0.8,
)
```

`strategy="top"` keeps the original lexical ranking and takes the first
candidate that passes the filters, `strategy="llm"` takes the LLM-selected
accepts, and `strategy="reviewed"` takes only rows whose `decision` column says
`accepted` — the shape `apply_sdp_semantics()` writes. **`"reviewed"` is exempt
from the unattended auto-apply gate**, and deliberately: that gate is a lexical
compatibility
heuristic for deciding whether a seeded top-1 hit is safe to write into a
dictionary nobody has looked at, and a human who read the definition and said
yes is the opposite situation. Running it there let a regex silently overrule an
explicit decision, with nothing said beyond a count of rows that "did not meet
the requested filters" (metasalmon backlog #118).

The four core roles — variable, property, entity, unit — are eligible for
automatic prefill in `create_sdp()` whenever a compatible candidate is found.
**Constraint and statistical modifier are eligible too, but only on the
deterministic path and only when the column's own name, label or description
carries the evidence** for the qualifier or the aggregation. The retrieval
offering a hit is never enough on its own: a `mean_wild_spawner_count` column
earns both slots, a bare `count` column earns neither, whatever comes back from
search.

Under LLM review (`llm_assess=True`) the two qualifier roles are excluded
outright, as the `roles=` argument above shows. A reviewed accept is not a
licence to auto-apply the roles that change what the variable *is*: a mean
weight and a maximum weight are different variables, which is why sdp-0.3.0
moved the modifier into the dictionary in the first place.

Everything prefilled is marked `REVIEW:`, including the two qualifier slots.
That marking is the point rather than a detail — an unmarked constraint IRI is
an unreviewed assertion sitting in a slot you never asked about.

::: {.callout-note}
This page said the opposite until 2026-08-24: that only the four core roles
were eligible and constraint and statistical modifier were left for explicit
review. That was a true description of this package and a false one of
metasalmon, whose deterministic path had always applied them under the same
evidence gates — and each side's prose matched its own code, so no reader was
positioned to catch it. Hub Q16 ruled metasalmon right ("Yeah lets go the R
way") and this package moved. See PARITY.md row 57.
:::

## The spreadsheet fallback {#the-spreadsheet-fallback}

Editing `metadata/*.csv` in a spreadsheet still works and is still supported.
Save the files back as CSV and reload with `read_salmon_datapackage()`.

It is the fallback for one reason: the only record of a decision made that way
is the mutated CSV. There is nothing saying which candidates were considered, on
what evidence the chosen one won, or that a slot was left blank deliberately —
which makes it the one unreproducible link in a chain that is otherwise
byte-reproducible, C-collated, hash-verified and guarded. `apply_sdp_semantics()`
and the `set_sdp_*()` setters write straight into the package, so with them there
is nothing to save or reload either.

`README-review.txt` in the package folder carries the same checklist, and
`metadata/column_dictionary.csv` is a reasonable `llm_context_files` input when
you want the LLM review step to reason from the package itself rather than a
separate methods note — pass the path string, not a DataFrame read from it, and
set `llm_assess=True`; context alone does not enable a provider call.

## Assemble the reviewed closure

**Strict validation is not the publication gate.** A package that passes
`validate_salmon_datapackage(require_iris=True)` can still be refused by
`write_eml_from_sdp()` and `publish_sdp_to_knb()`, because the EML/KNB path
additionally requires a **reviewed closure**: a standing record of which
vocabulary terms you accepted, on what evidence, and for which target.

Three files carry it. **`write_sdp_semantic_closure()` writes the first two and
pins the digests the third one carries**; the reviewed EML facts in the third
are yours.

| File | What it must contain | Written by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `metadata/semantic_vocabulary.csv` | One evidence row per canonical measurement IRI — exactly that set, no more and no less | `write_sdp_semantic_closure()` |
| `reviewed_semantic_selections.csv` | Exactly one `accepted` row per canonical review target | `write_sdp_semantic_closure()` |
| `metadata/eml-mapping.yml` | The reviewed EML facts, plus the SHA-256 of each of the two files above | you, except the two SHA-256 values |

**The canonical measurement IRI set** is every non-empty value across
`term_iri`, `property_iri`, `entity_iri`, `constraint_iri`,
`statistical_modifier_iri` and `unit_iri` on your `measurement` dictionary rows,
plus any `tables.csv` `method_iri` and any procedure IRIs reached through
`codes.csv` from an observation-structures binding.

**The canonical review target set** is derived independently, and it is *not*
the measurement set plus anything. It is every slot a reviewer decided: the same
six semantic fields on your `measurement` dictionary rows, plus each table's
`observation_unit_iri` **and** its `method_iri`.

**The two sets differ in both directions**, which is why neither can be reasoned
from the other:

* an `observation_unit_iri` is a **review target and not a vocabulary term** — a
  reviewed selection, but not something the EML measurement path emits; and
* a `sosa:usedProcedure` reached through a code value is a **vocabulary term and
  not a review target** — the EML method path emits it, but no reviewer ever
  selected it as a slot, because it comes from the data rather than from a
  metadata field.

Getting that second direction backwards is worth avoiding rather than
discovering: the ledger gate accepts **exactly** the canonical target set, so a
row added for a code-resolved procedure is refused as unexpected, and the
package stops validating because of a row you added to make it validate.

### Produce both files

`write_sdp_semantic_closure()` derives both canonical sets, re-runs
`find_terms()` for each IRI to resolve its evidence, computes every
`reviewed_snapshot_sha256`, writes both files, and rewrites the two file digests
in `metadata/eml-mapping.yml`. **No SHA-256 in a reviewed package is ever
hand-written.**

Two kinds of value it cannot derive, and both go in `evidence`:

* **Vocabularies `find_terms()` cannot search.** It resolves `smn` and `gcdfo`.
  A QUDT unit row is hand-authored in full. It also cannot fill `native_type` or
  `source_url`, which describe the ontology *artifact* rather than the term;
  those are derived from the resolved source and can be overridden.
* **`confidence` and `review_rationale`**, which are your judgement. They are
  read from `semantic_suggestions.csv` where `apply_sdp_semantics()` recorded a
  decision reason, and otherwise written as a `REVIEW REQUIRED:` marker with a
  warning naming each target that got one. Replace those before publishing.
  A `reject_suggestion(..., reason=…)` you wrote during the review is what ends
  up there, which is the second thing that reason buys you.

```python
import pandas as pd

from metasalmonpy import write_sdp_semantic_closure

# Your judgement on each accepted IRI. The term evidence is resolved for you.
judgements = pd.DataFrame([
    {
        "iri": "https://w3id.org/gcdfo/salmon#SpawnerAbundance",
        "confidence": "high",
        "review_rationale": "The column is an escapement estimate of adult spawners.",
    },
    {
        "iri": "https://w3id.org/smn/Observation",
        "confidence": "high",
        "review_rationale": "Each row is one population-year observation.",
    },
])

# A QUDT row is hand-authored end to end: the search cannot reach QUDT.
qudt = pd.DataFrame([{
    "iri": "https://qudt.org/vocab/unit/INDIV",
    "label": "Individual",
    "definition": "A counting unit denoting one organism.",
    "source": "qudt",
    "ontology": "qudt",
    "resource_kind": "Unit",
    "type_iris": "http://qudt.org/schema/qudt/Unit",
    "native_type": "qudt:Unit",
    "source_url": "https://qudt.org/vocab/unit/",
    "confidence": "high",
    "review_rationale": "Values are whole counts of organisms.",
}])

closure = write_sdp_semantic_closure(
    "path/to/package",
    evidence=pd.concat([judgements, qudt], ignore_index=True),
)
```

Copy the reviewed EML sidecar template **before** running this, so the two
digests are pinned in the same pass. If you produce the closure first, run it
again once the sidecar exists.

### Three outcomes, and only one of them is an ontology gap

**An IRI it cannot resolve is reported, not guessed at, and not fatal.**
`closure["gaps"]` is a term-gap table in the same shape
`detect_semantic_term_gaps()` returns, so it feeds the request pipeline
directly:

```python
from metasalmonpy import render_ontology_term_request, submit_term_request_issues

if len(closure["gaps"]) > 0:
    requests = render_ontology_term_request(closure["gaps"], ask=False)
    submit_term_request_issues(requests, dry_run=True)
```

The unresolved row is left out of the vocabulary rather than invented, and the
omission is not silent: attempting EML export names the same IRI as missing.

The other two ways a row can go unwritten are **not** gaps, because in neither
case is the term known to be absent — and reporting either as a gap would ask an
ontology to mint a term nobody established was missing:

* **A lookup that did not answer** — a search that raised, or a `find_terms()`
  result whose `attrs["diagnostics"]` records a source that failed. Nothing has
  been learned about that IRI, so the call raises `RuntimeError` and **writes
  nothing**, naming each IRI and the sources that did not answer. The remedy is
  to re-run; leaving a half-derived closure on disk would make the retry start
  from worse state.
* **A term found with incomplete evidence** — an exact IRI hit carrying a blank
  required field, which a class with no definition is the ordinary case of. The
  row appears in `closure["incomplete"]`, naming the missing field and the slot,
  with a warning; every other row is still written. Supply the field through
  `evidence`, or annotate the term in its ontology.

Reading a package with an existing closure, the whole thing round-trips: the two
files this writes are exactly the two `write_eml_from_sdp()` and
`publish_sdp_to_knb()` read back.
